name: Lip stencil / bone structure hack: orthotropics for lip support

lead: In mewing and orthotropics circles, the idea is that holding a tongue and jaw posture can change the bone beneath the lips, giving better lip support and a more balanced profile.

Mewing is oral posture training associated with orthodontist John Mew and his son Mike Mew, built on pressing the tongue against the palate. Reference sources describe it as unproven, say the American Association of Orthodontists sees no evidence it improves the jaw, and do not address lips or soft-tissue profile.

paras: Practitioners rest the tongue against the palate, keep the lips sealed and breathe through the nose, as a constant background habit maintained over months or years.
Potential risks cited include jaw joint problems, bite changes and delayed orthodontic care in children.

angle.text: Mewing and orthotropics circles say tongue posture can reshape the bone under the lips to improve profile. The posture is held daily, and followers expect better lip support over time. Reference sources describe mewing as unproven and do not cover lips.

lead: This entry covers the claim, circulated in mewing and orthotropics circles, that jaw and facial posture training can change the profile of the lips by altering the bone structure that supports them. Mewing is a form of oral posture training associated with orthodontist John Mew and his son Mike Mew, built on tongue pressure against the palate.[1]

The reference sources reviewed describe mewing as unproven, state that the American Association of Orthodontists sees no evidence that it improves the jaw, and do not address lips or soft-tissue profile specifically.[1][2]

paras: Orthotropics holds that oral posture guides jaw and facial growth, in contrast to conventional orthodontics, which focuses on aligning teeth.[2] The lip-related claim extends this: if the jaws move forward or the upper jaw widens, the lips are said to gain support and a different profile. The reference articles do not describe lip outcomes from mewing.

The American Association of Orthodontists and the Cleveland Clinic are reported to state that there is no credible scientific evidence that mewing reshapes the face or jawline.[2] A reference article states that no credible research has proven the efficacy of orthotropics.[1] Potential risks cited for the practice include temporomandibular joint disorders, bite problems and delayed orthodontic care in children.[2]

No studies found on orthotropics or mewing changing lip profile. Related work exists on orofacial myofunctional therapy: 2025 pilot studies reported effects on hyoid position and jaw pain, but they did not directly test mewing or lip outcomes.[2]

lore.intro: Mewing communities discuss lip support as one possible by-product of posture training, alongside jawline and midface claims.

claims.claim: Mewing can change lip profile by moving the underlying bone structure.
